```{webr}
#| context: setup

library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_gray(base_size = 14))
survey <- read_csv("data/sleep_survey.csv")
```

## Where we left off

::: {.callout-important title="Recall from Lecture 15"}
A model with one predictor gives a **slope**: the change in the predicted `y` when `x` goes up by 1 unit. We also learned to stay inside the **observed range** when predicting.
:::

At the end of last class, you fit `avg_grade ~ study_hours_week`. Did the result surprise you?

Today we give the model more **structure**:

- add a categorical predictor
- check the fit with residuals
- use more than one numeric predictor, and watch out for **multicollinearity**


# The puzzle

## Does studying help?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(survey, aes(x = study_hours_week, y = avg_grade)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Study (hours per week)", y = "Average grade (%)")
```

The line is flat, or even slightly downward. Does studying not help?

## Look at the subgroups

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.8
ggplot(survey, aes(x = study_hours_week, y = avg_grade, color = program)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = lm, se = FALSE,
              color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Study (hours per week)", y = "Average grade (%)")
```

The dashed black line is the pooled fit from the last slide. The coloured lines are **one per program**.

::: {.callout-caution title="Checkpoint"}
Within each program, which way does the line go? Why does the dashed line disagree?
:::

## Why the disagreement? {.smaller}

```{r}
survey |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarise(mean_study = mean(study_hours_week),
            mean_grade = mean(avg_grade),
            n = n())
```

- Programs that study **more** tend to have **lower** average grades.
- Across all students, that between-program difference hides the within-program pattern.

::: {.callout-important title="Confounding"}
A **third variable** (here, `program`) is linked to both the predictor and the outcome. Ignoring it can hide a relationship, exaggerate one, or even flip its direction.
:::


# Adding a categorical predictor

## A categorical predictor

```{r}
class(survey$program)
unique(survey$program)
```

`program` is text with five possible values. Most model functions cannot use text directly, so R turns it into numbers behind the scenes.

## Indicator (dummy) variables {.smaller}

R creates a 0/1 column for each program **except one**:

| program | Business | Engineering | Health Sci | Science |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Business | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Engineering | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Health Sci | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Science | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

::: {.callout-note title="Reference level"}
The left-out program is the **reference level**. R uses the first one alphabetically, here Arts. Every other program is compared with it.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Checkpoint"}
If a variable had **eight** categories, how many indicator columns would R create?
:::

## Adding `program` to the formula

```r
avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program
```

::: {.callout-warning title="The + is not arithmetic"}
`study_hours_week + program` does **not** add the two values together. It lists two separate predictors, each with its own coefficient.
:::

## Fit it

```{r}
program_fit <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program, data = survey)
program_fit
```

Compare the `study_hours_week` slope with the pooled one from earlier.

## Reading the coefficients {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip title="The study slope"}
For two students **in the same program**, each extra hour of weekly study goes with this much change in predicted average grade. The comparison is "other things held fixed".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="The program coefficients"}
Each one (for example `programEngineering`) is the **difference from the reference level**, Arts. It compares students with the **same** study hours, so it shifts the whole line up or down.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Recall: the intercept"}
The intercept is the predicted grade for an **Arts** student who studies **0 hours**. Check whether 0 is a realistic value before reading too much into it.
:::

## One slope, parallel lines

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.8
survey |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(program_fit)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = study_hours_week, y = avg_grade, color = program)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Study (hours per week)", y = "Average grade (%)")
```

Every program shares the **same slope** but has its **own starting point**. Is that a realistic structure?

## Your turn: pooled vs. adjusted {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
1. Fit `avg_grade ~ study_hours_week`. Write down the slope.
2. Fit `avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program`. Write down the slope.
3. Why did the slope change? Explain it in one sentence using the word *confounding*.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: pooled_vs_adjusted

pooled_fit   <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week, data = survey)
adjusted_fit <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program, data = survey)

coef(pooled_fit)
coef(adjusted_fit)
```

## A p-value, in plain words

If you run `summary()` on a model, you will see a p-value column.

```{r}
summary(program_fit)
```

::: {.callout-note title="How to read it, without the maths"}
A small p-value means a pattern this clear would be **unlikely to appear by pure chance**. It does not tell you the model fits well, and it does not tell you the relationship is causal.
:::


# Checking the fit

## Why check the fit?

A model gives you numbers whether or not the model is a good description. **Residual plots** help us see whether the structure we chose fits the data.

::: {.callout-caution title="Checkpoint"}
What would a *bad* residual plot look like? Think about curves, funnels, and isolated points.
:::

## Residuals vs. fitted values

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
survey |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(program_fit), resid = resid(program_fit)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (predicted grade)", y = "Residual")
```

We want a shapeless cloud around zero: no curve, no funnel. Which points look unusual?


# Several numeric predictors

## More than one numeric predictor

Predictors do not have to be categorical. You can add as many as you like:

```r
avg_grade ~ sleep_hours + sleep_quality
```

::: {.callout-note title="Holding the others fixed"}
Each slope now means: the change in predicted `y` for a 1-unit increase in that predictor, **with the other predictors held fixed**.
:::

But what if two predictors measure almost the same thing?

## Multicollinearity {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="Multicollinearity"}
Two or more predictors that **move closely together**. Because they carry overlapping information, the model cannot tell which one deserves the credit.
:::

Think of two friends who always give you the **same advice**. If a decision turns out well, who gets the credit?

When predictors overlap a lot:

- the **individual slopes** become unstable and hard to interpret
- a slope can even change **size or sign** when you add or drop another predictor
- the model's overall **predictions** can still be fine

## Spot it before you model

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
cor(survey$sleep_hours, survey$sleep_quality)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = sleep_hours, y = sleep_quality)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Sleep (hours per night)", y = "Sleep quality (1 to 5)")
```

Students who sleep longer also rate their sleep as better. The two predictors **overlap**.

## Watch the coefficients

```{r}
coef(lm(avg_grade ~ sleep_hours, data = survey))
coef(lm(avg_grade ~ sleep_quality, data = survey))
coef(lm(avg_grade ~ sleep_hours + sleep_quality, data = survey))
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Checkpoint"}
Compare each predictor's slope **alone** with its slope **together**. What happened to `sleep_quality`? Is the new value easy to explain?
:::

## What to do about it {.smaller}

- **Check** how strongly your predictors correlate with each other *before* modelling
- **Choose one** of the overlapping predictors, or **combine** them into a single measure
- **Be careful** reading individual slopes when predictors overlap
- Remember: multicollinearity is about the **predictors**, not the outcome

::: {.callout-warning title="Not the same as confounding"}
Confounding is a third variable tied to both the predictor and the outcome. Multicollinearity is two **predictors** tied to each other. Both make slopes harder to read.
:::

## Your turn {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
1. Look at the correlations among the numeric columns: `sleep_hours`, `sleep_quality`, `stress_level`, `study_hours_week`, `num_courses`, `work_hours_week`. Which pairs overlap the most?
2. Fit `avg_grade ~ sleep_hours + stress_level`. Compare the slopes with those from the models using each predictor alone.
3. Would you worry about multicollinearity here?
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: collinearity

survey |>
  select(sleep_hours, sleep_quality, stress_level,
         study_hours_week, num_courses, work_hours_week) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)

coef(lm(avg_grade ~ sleep_hours, data = survey))
coef(lm(avg_grade ~ stress_level, data = survey))
coef(lm(avg_grade ~ sleep_hours + stress_level, data = survey))
```


# Predicting with structure

## `predict()` with a categorical predictor

Pass the program as **text**, matching the original names. R builds the indicator columns for you.

```{r}
new_students <- data.frame(
  study_hours_week = c(10, 10, 20, 20),
  program = c("Arts", "Engineering", "Arts", "Engineering")
)
predict(program_fit, new_students)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Same machinery for new data"}
The formula applies the same encoding to new data as it did to the data we used to fit the model.
:::

## Stay inside the range

```{r}
range(survey$study_hours_week)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Recall: extrapolation"}
Predictions are only as trustworthy as new data is similar to the data used to fit the model. Most students study between about 12 and 19 hours a week. The few students far beyond that deserve a second look.
:::

## Your turn {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
1. Predict the average grade for a **Science** student who studies 15 hours a week.
2. Predict it for a **Business** student with the same study hours.
3. How much do the two predictions differ? Where in the model output could you have found that?
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: structured_predict

program_fit <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program, data = survey)

new_students <- data.frame(
  study_hours_week = c(15, 15),
  program = c("Science", "Business")
)
predict(program_fit, new_students)
```


# The formula as structure

## What does the formula do?

The R formula usually does **three jobs** at once:

1. It defines **which columns** the model uses
2. It **encodes** those columns into numbers (for example, indicator columns)
3. It defines each column's **role** (outcome or predictor)

When you write `avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program`, you are mostly thinking about job 3. The formula also quietly did job 2: it created the four indicator columns for `program`.

## Summary {.smaller}

- A **confounding** variable can hide or flip a relationship, so check subgroups
- A categorical predictor becomes **indicator columns**; the first level is the **reference level**
- With several predictors, each slope means "other things held fixed"
- **Residual plots** help us check whether the structure fits
- **Multicollinearity**: overlapping predictors make individual slopes unstable
- Stay inside the **observed range** when predicting

Next: how do we know a model works on data it has not seen?
